listitem.para: Restrict to (the complement of) a geometry &Z_support;
The geometry must be in 2D and the computation with respect to it is done in 2D. The result preserves the Z dimension of the temporal point, if it exists.

A geodetic point is restricted to a geography, which must be a polygon or a multipolygon, and the computation is done on the sphere: the point travels the great circle between two positions and the region is bounded by the great circles through its own vertices, so the trip enters and leaves where those paths cross. The difference grows with latitude, a trip along a parallel standing well to the north of it.
Restrict to (the complement of) an stbox &Z_support;
listitem.programlisting: atStbox(tgeom,stbox,borderInc boolean=true) → tgeompoint minusStbox(tgeom,stbox,borderInc boolean=true) → tgeompoint
listitem.para: The third optional argument is used for multidimensional tiling (see ) to exclude the upper border of the tiles when a temporal value is split in multiple tiles, so that all fragments of the temporal geometry are exclusive.

A temporal point is restricted in 3D. The Z dimension is taken into account only when both the temporal point and the box have it, so that 2D and 3D arguments can be mixed, and the result preserves the Z dimension of the temporal point. The body of a temporal geometry is instead clipped in 2D: a box holding coordinates refuses a temporal geometry having Z dimension, while a box holding only a period restricts it in time as for any other temporal type. The restriction of a tgeography to a spatiotemporal box is not implemented.

A geodetic temporal point travels the great circle between two positions, and the box holds it where that circle enters and leaves the box: a trip from Point(10 60) to Point(50 60) reaches latitude 61.518762, and a trip across the antimeridian sweeps the longitudes the short way round. Two boxes meeting at a crossing state the same instant for it, so the pieces of a trip hold the period of the trip and its positions.
Restrict to (the complement of) an elevation span &Z_support;

The elevation of a temporal point is its Z coordinate, which runs linearly in time whether the point is planar or geodetic, so the periods the span admits are the same for both. The positions at the bounds of those periods are not: a geodetic point travels the great circle between two positions and reaches the elevation of a bound there rather than on the straight line in longitude and latitude.
Return or set the spatial reference identifier &Z_support; &geography_support;
Transform to a spatial reference identifier &Z_support; &geography_support;
listitem.programlisting: transform(tspatial,integer) → tspatial transformPipeline(tspatial,pipeline text,srid integer, is_forward boolean=true) → tspatial transformPipeline(geo,pipeline text,srid integer, is_forward boolean=true) → geo
listitem.para: The function transformPipeline transforms a geometry or a geography with a pipeline in the same way.
The transform function specifies the transformation with a target SRID. An error is raised when the input temporal point has an unknown SRID (represented by 0).
The transformPipeline function specifies the transformation with a defined coordinate transformation pipeline represented with the following string format:

The SRID of the input temporal point is ignored, and the SRID of the output temporal point will be set to zero unless a value is provided via the optional srid parameter. As stated by the last parameter, the pipeline is executed by default in a forward direction; by setting the parameter to false, the pipeline is executed in the inverse direction.
listitem.programlisting: WITH test(tgeo, pipeline) AS ( SELECT tgeogpoint 'SRID=4326;{Point(4.3525 50.846667 100.0)@2001-01-01, Point(-0.1275 51.507222 100.0)@2001-01-02}', text 'urn:ogc:def:coordinateOperation:EPSG::16031' ) SELECT asEWKT(transformPipeline(transformPipeline(tgeo, pipeline, 4326), pipeline, 4326, false), 6) FROM test; /* SRID=4326;{POINT Z (4.3525 50.846667 100)@2001-01-01, POINT Z (-0.1275 51.507222 100)@2001-01-02} */

listitem.para: Return the spatiotemporal bounding box expanded in the spatial dimension by a float value &Z_support; &geography_support;

sect1.title: Distance Operations

listitem.para: Return the smallest distance ever &Z_support; &geography_support;
For geographies, the operator computes on the WGS 84 spheroid, and the function nearestApproachDistance computes on the sphere, faster, if its last argument is false.

The operator |=| can be used for doing nearest neighbor searches using a GiST or an SP-GiST index (see ). This operator corresponds to the PostGIS function ST_DistanceCPA, altough the latter requires both arguments to be a trajectory.

When one argument is a spatiotemporal box carrying a period, the distance is measured from the part of the temporal value inside that period, and the result is NULL when no part of it is. A box carrying no period measures the whole temporal value.
listitem.programlisting: SELECT ST_DistanceCPA(tgeompoint '[Point(0 0 0)@2001-01-01, Point(1 1 1)@2001-01-03, Point(0 0 0)@2001-01-05)'::geometry, tgeompoint '[Point(2 0 0)@2001-01-02, Point(1 1 1)@2001-01-04, Point(2 2 2)@2001-01-06)'::geometry); -- 0.5

listitem.para: Return the instant of the first temporal point at which the two arguments are at the nearest distance &Z_support; &geography_support;

The function will only return the first instant that it finds if there are more than one. The resulting instant may be at an exclusive bound. For geographies, the closest points of each segment are located on the sphere and their distances are compared on the WGS 84 spheroid by default, as the PostGIS function ST_Distance measures a geography distance. If the last argument is false, they are compared on the sphere.

Function nearestApproachInstant generalizes the PostGIS function ST_ClosestPointOfApproach. First, the latter function requires both arguments to be trajectories. Second, function nearestApproachInstant returns both the point and the timestamp of the nearest point of approach while the PostGIS function only provides the timestamp as shown next.
listitem.programlisting: SELECT to_timestamp(ST_ClosestPointOfApproach( tgeompoint '[Point(0 0 0)@2001-01-01, Point(1 1 1)@2001-01-03, Point(0 0 0)@2001-01-05)'::geometry, tgeompoint '[Point(2 0 0)@2001-01-02, Point(1 1 1)@2001-01-04, Point(2 2 2)@2001-01-06)'::geometry)); -- 2001-01-03 12:00:00

listitem.para: Return the minimum spatial distance between two sets of temporal geometries, ignoring time

The distance is measured between the trajectories with time discarded, equal to ST_Distance of the trajectory of each argument, and the result is the minimum over every pair drawn from the two sets. Two values that follow the same path at different times are therefore at distance zero. The time-synchronous quantity, which compares two arguments only at the instants they share, is nearestApproachDistance. A single pair is the one-element case. For geographies, the computation is done on the WGS 84 spheroid by default. If the last argument is false, a faster spherical calculation is used.
listitem.programlisting: SELECT minDistance(ARRAY[tgeompoint '[Point(0 0)@2001-01-01, Point(1 1)@2001-01-03)', tgeompoint '[Point(5 5)@2001-01-01, Point(6 6)@2001-01-03)'], ARRAY[tgeompoint '[Point(0 1)@2001-01-01, Point(1 0)@2001-01-03)']); -- 0 SELECT round(minDistance( ARRAY[tgeogpoint '[Point(0 1)@2001-01-01, Point(0 2)@2001-01-02]'], ARRAY[tgeogpoint 'Point(0 0)@2001-01-01'], false)::numeric, 3); -- 111195.080

listitem.para: Return the line connecting the nearest approach point &Z_support; &geography_support;

The function will only return the first line that it finds if there are more than one. For geographies, the line joins the points at the nearest approach instant, which the WGS 84 spheroid decides by default and the sphere if the last argument is false.
Function shortestLine can be used to obtain the result provided by the PostGIS function ST_CPAWithin when both arguments are trajectories as shown next.
listitem.programlisting: SELECT ST_Length(shortestLine( tgeompoint '[Point(0 0 0)@2001-01-01, Point(1 1 1)@2001-01-03, Point(0 0 0)@2001-01-05)', tgeompoint '[Point(2 0 0)@2001-01-02, Point(1 1 1)@2001-01-04, Point(2 2 2)@2001-01-06)')) <= 0.5; -- true SELECT ST_CPAWithin(tgeompoint '[Point(0 0 0)@2001-01-01, Point(1 1 1)@2001-01-03, Point(0 0 0)@2001-01-05)'::geometry, tgeompoint '[Point(2 0 0)@2001-01-02, Point(1 1 1)@2001-01-04, Point(2 2 2)@2001-01-06)'::geometry, 0.5); -- true

sect1.para: The temporal distance operator, denoted <->, computes the distance at each instant of the intersection of the temporal extents of their arguments and results in a temporal float. Computing temporal distance is useful in many mobility applications. For example, a moving cluster (also known as convoy or flock) is defined as a set of objects that move close to each other for a long time interval. This requires to compute temporal distance between two moving objects.

A temporal point with linear interpolation takes as its other argument a temporal point, a point, or, when it is planar and 2D, a geometry of any other type. A temporal point of any other interpolation, an instant included, has a value at its instants only, and takes any geometry or geography, its distance at each instant being the distance of the point to it. Notice that the temporal types only consider linear interpolation between values, while the distance is a root of a quadratic function. Therefore, the temporal distance operator gives a linear approximation of the actual distance value for temporal sequence points. In this case, the arguments are synchronized in the time dimension, and for each of the composing line segments of the arguments, the spatial distance between the start point, the end point, and the nearest point of approach is computed, as shown in the examples below.

listitem.para: Return the temporal distance &Z_support; &geography_support;
For geographies, the operator computes on the WGS 84 spheroid, and the function tDistance computes on the sphere, faster, if its last argument is false.

sect1.title: Planar and Geodetic Computations
sect1.para: The coordinates of a temporal geometry (tgeometry or tgeompoint) are interpreted in the plane of their spatial reference system, and those of a temporal geography (tgeography or tgeogpoint) as longitudes and latitudes on the WGS 84 ellipsoid. Which operations a temporal geography supports, and how exactly, follows from three rules.

listitem.para: An operation is available for geographies when it is defined on the ellipsoid. This is the case of the metric operations, such as the distance, the distance within, the length, the area, the azimuth, or the centroid, which are computed on the WGS 84 spheroid, or on the sphere, faster, when their argument spheroid is false. It is also the case of the intersection and the disjointness, since two geographies intersect when their distance is zero. It is not the case of contains, covers, and touches, which are defined by the dimensionally extended nine-intersection model of planar topology, nor of the planar constructions, such as the union or the intersection of two geometries, which PostGIS does not define for geographies either. These functions raise an error for geographies.

The ever, always, and temporal versions of an operation available for geographies are computed exactly. The value of a temporal geography, and of a temporal geography point with discrete or step interpolation, is constant between two instants, so the operation is evaluated at each instant. A temporal geography point with linear interpolation moves along a great circle between two instants, and the result of a temporal relationship changes at the instants at which its geodetic distance to the other argument crosses the given distance. These instants are computed when the other argument is a geography point or a temporal geography point. For other geographies, such as lines and polygons, the temporal relationships tIntersects, tDisjoint, and tDwithin of a temporal geography point with linear interpolation raise an error.
A temporal relationship available for geographies accepts a geography or a temporal geography on either side, as its planar version accepts a geometry or a temporal geometry.

sect1.para: A temporal geometry in SRID 4326 is converted into a temporal geography with the same values by the cast ::tgeography, and back by the cast ::tgeometry. The function transform reprojects it instead into a planar spatial reference system whose unit is the meter, in which distances and areas are planar.
sect1.programlisting: SELECT round(nearestApproachDistance(tgeometry 'SRID=4326;[Polygon((4.35 50.84, 4.40 50.84,4.40 50.88,4.35 50.84))@2001-01-01, Point(4.37 50.85)@2001-01-02]', geometry 'SRID=4326;Point(4.45 50.84)')::numeric, 4); -- 0.0500 SELECT round(nearestApproachDistance(tgeometry 'SRID=4326;[Polygon((4.35 50.84, 4.40 50.84,4.40 50.88,4.35 50.84))@2001-01-01, Point(4.37 50.85)@2001-01-02]' ::tgeography, geography 'Point(4.45 50.84)')::numeric, 1); -- 3521.9

sect1.title: Ever and Always Relationships
sect1.para: Each relationship of this section has two forms. The scalar form compares two values, a geometry or a temporal geometry on each side, and returns whether the relationship holds at some instant (prefix e, ever) or at every instant (prefix a, always) of the time they share. The array form, whose name ends in Pairs, compares every element of an array of temporal geometries with every element of another and returns, one row per pair, the one-based indexes i and j of the pairs for which the scalar form returns true. A pair sharing no instant, for which the scalar form returns null, is not returned. The array form states in a single call the spatial join of two sets of moving objects, which the scalar form states by comparing every pair of their cross product: the spatiotemporal box of each element settles the pairs whose boxes alone decide the relationship, and the relationship is computed exactly on the others. The indexes are positions in the arrays, and an array_agg of the identifiers in the order of the array of values maps them back to the objects. The array form is defined for temporal points and temporal geometries, planar and geodetic, where the scalar form is, except touches, whose array form takes temporal geometries. Contains and covers have the scalar form only.

The following example returns, for each pair of ships, whether they ever come within a distance of 2 of each other, first with the scalar form on two of them, then with the array form on all of them, mapping the indexes back to the identifiers.
sect1.programlisting: SELECT eDwithin(tgeompoint '[Point(0 0)@2001-01-01, Point(0 10)@2001-01-02]', tgeompoint '[Point(1 0)@2001-01-01, Point(1 10)@2001-01-02]', 2); -- true WITH ships(id, trip) AS (VALUES ('A', tgeompoint '[Point(0 0)@2001-01-01, Point(0 10)@2001-01-02]'), ('B', tgeompoint '[Point(50 50)@2001-01-01, Point(50 60)@2001-01-02]'), ('C', tgeompoint '[Point(1 0)@2001-01-01, Point(1 10)@2001-01-02]')), fleet AS (SELECT array_agg(id ORDER BY id) AS ids, array_agg(trip ORDER BY id) AS trips FROM ships) SELECT ids[i] AS ship1, ids[j] AS ship2 FROM fleet, eDwithinPairs(trips, trips, 2) WHERE i < j; -- A | C

listitem.para: Ever or always contains

This function returns true if the temporal geometry and the geometry ever or always intersect at their interior. Recall that a geometry does not contain things in its boundary and thus, polygons and lines do not contain lines and points lying in their boundary. Please refer to the documentation of the ST_Contains function in PostGIS.
Ever or always covers
Please refer to the documentation of the ST_Contains and the ST_Covers function in PostGIS for detailed explanations about the difference between the two functions.
Is ever or always disjoint &Z_support; &geography_support;
listitem.programlisting: eDisjoint({geo,tgeo},{geo,tgeo}) → boolean aDisjoint({geo,tgeo},{geo,tgeo}) → boolean eDisjointPairs(tgeo[],tgeo[]) → setof(i integer,j integer) aDisjointPairs(tgeo[],tgeo[]) → setof(i integer,j integer)
listitem.para: The array form returns the pairs that are ever or always disjoint. In the following examples, the first trip of the second array crosses the trip of the first array, which is ever but not always disjoint from it.
listitem.programlisting: SELECT i, j FROM eDisjointPairs( ARRAY[tgeompoint '[Point(0 0)@2001-01-01, Point(0 10)@2001-01-02]'], ARRAY[tgeompoint '[Point(5 0)@2001-01-01, Point(-5 10)@2001-01-02]', tgeompoint '[Point(0 0)@2001-01-01, Point(0 10)@2001-01-02]']); -- 1 | 1 SELECT i, j FROM aDisjointPairs( ARRAY[tgeompoint '[Point(0 0)@2001-01-01, Point(0 10)@2001-01-02]'], ARRAY[tgeompoint '[Point(5 0)@2001-01-01, Point(-5 10)@2001-01-02]', tgeompoint '[Point(5 0)@2001-01-01, Point(5 10)@2001-01-02]']); -- 1 | 2

listitem.para: Is ever or always at distance within &Z_support; &geography_support;
listitem.programlisting: eDwithin({geo,tgeo},{geo,tgeo},float) → boolean aDwithin({geometry,tgeom},{geometry,tgeom},float) → boolean eDwithin({geography,tgeog},{geography,tgeog},float,spheroid boolean=true) → boolean aDwithin(tgeog,tgeog,float,spheroid boolean=true) → boolean eDwithinPairs(tgeom[],tgeom[],float) → setof(i integer,j integer) aDwithinPairs(tgeom[],tgeom[],float) → setof(i integer,j integer) eDwithinPairs(tgeog[],tgeog[],float,spheroid boolean=true) → setof(i integer,j integer) aDwithinPairs(tgeog[],tgeog[],float,spheroid boolean=true) → setof(i integer,j integer)
listitem.para: For geographies, the computation is done on the WGS 84 spheroid by default. If the last argument is false, a faster spherical calculation is used.

The array form returns the pairs that are ever or always within the distance. For geographies, as for the scalar form, the distance is measured on the WGS 84 spheroid by default and on the sphere if the last argument is false.
listitem.programlisting: SELECT i, j FROM aDwithinPairs( ARRAY[tgeompoint '[Point(0 0)@2001-01-01, Point(0 10)@2001-01-02]'], ARRAY[tgeompoint '[Point(1 0)@2001-01-01, Point(1 10)@2001-01-02]', tgeompoint '[Point(1 0)@2001-01-01, Point(5 10)@2001-01-02]'], 2); -- 1 | 1 SELECT i, j FROM eDwithinPairs( ARRAY[tgeogpoint '[Point(0 1)@2001-01-01, Point(0 2)@2001-01-02]'], ARRAY[tgeogpoint '[Point(0 0)@2001-01-01, Point(0 0)@2001-01-02]'], 110800); -- 1 | 1 SELECT count(*) FROM eDwithinPairs( ARRAY[tgeogpoint '[Point(0 1)@2001-01-01, Point(0 2)@2001-01-02]'], ARRAY[tgeogpoint '[Point(0 0)@2001-01-01, Point(0 0)@2001-01-02]'], 110800, false); -- 0

listitem.para: Ever or always intersects &Z_support; &geography_support;
listitem.programlisting: eIntersects({geo,tgeo},{geo,tgeo}) → boolean aIntersects({geometry,tgeom},{geometry,tgeom}) → boolean eIntersectsPairs(tgeo[],tgeo[]) → setof(i integer,j integer) aIntersectsPairs(tgeo[],tgeo[]) → setof(i integer,j integer)
listitem.para: The array form returns the pairs that ever or always intersect. Two temporal points always intersect when they are equal at every instant they share.
listitem.programlisting: SELECT i, j FROM eIntersectsPairs( ARRAY[tgeompoint '[Point(0 0)@2001-01-01, Point(2 2)@2001-01-03]'], ARRAY[tgeompoint '[Point(0 0)@2001-01-01, Point(2 2)@2001-01-03]', tgeompoint '[Point(0 2)@2001-01-01, Point(2 0)@2001-01-03]', tgeompoint '[Point(5 5)@2001-01-01, Point(6 6)@2001-01-03]']); -- 1 | 1 -- 1 | 2 SELECT i, j FROM aIntersectsPairs( ARRAY[tgeompoint '[Point(0 0)@2001-01-01, Point(2 2)@2001-01-03]'], ARRAY[tgeompoint '[Point(0 0)@2001-01-01, Point(2 2)@2001-01-03]', tgeompoint '[Point(0 2)@2001-01-01, Point(2 0)@2001-01-03]', tgeompoint '[Point(5 5)@2001-01-01, Point(6 6)@2001-01-03]']); -- 1 | 1

listitem.para: Ever or always touches
listitem.programlisting: eTouches({geometry,tgeom},{geometry,tgeom}) → boolean aTouches({geometry,tgeom},{geometry,tgeom}) → boolean eTouchesPairs(tgeometry[],tgeometry[]) → setof(i integer,j integer) aTouchesPairs(tgeometry[],tgeometry[]) → setof(i integer,j integer)
listitem.para: The array form returns the pairs of temporal geometries that ever or always touch. In the following examples, the first geometry of the second array touches the geometry of the first array until it moves away on 2001-01-02.

sect1.title: Spatiotemporal Relationships
sect1.para: The disjoint, distance within, intersects and touches relationships also have an array form, whose name ends in Pairs, as the ever and always relationships of do. It compares every element of an array of temporal geometries with every element of another and returns, one row per pair whose temporal relationship is ever true, the one-based indexes i and j of the pair and the periods periods during which the relationship is true.

listitem.para: Temporal contains
Temporal disjoint &Z_support; &geography_support;
listitem.programlisting: tDisjoint({geo,tgeo},{geo,tgeo}) → tbool tDisjointPairs(tgeo[],tgeo[]) → setof(i integer,j integer,periods tstzspanset)
listitem.para: The function is the negation of tIntersects. Geographies are supported as stated in .
The array form returns the pairs that are disjoint at some instant, with the periods during which they are disjoint.
Temporal distance within &Z_support; &geography_support;
listitem.programlisting: tDwithin({geo,tgeo},{geo,tgeo},float) → tbool tDwithin({geography,tgeog},{geography,tgeog},float,spheroid boolean=true) → tbool tDwithinPairs(tgeom[],tgeom[],float) → setof(i integer,j integer,periods tstzspanset)
listitem.para: Geographies are supported as stated in : for a temporal geography point with linear interpolation, the other argument is a geography point or a temporal geography point. The distance is measured on the WGS 84 spheroid by default. If the last argument is false, it is measured on the sphere. A segment of a temporal geography point moves along a great circle, and the result changes its value at every instant at which the geodetic distance crosses the given distance, which a segment may cross several times.
The array form returns the pairs that are within the distance at some instant, with the periods during which they are within it.
Temporal intersects &Z_support; &geography_support;
listitem.programlisting: tIntersects({geo,tgeo},{geo,tgeo}) → tbool tIntersectsPairs(tgeo[],tgeo[]) → setof(i integer,j integer,periods tstzspanset)
listitem.para: Two temporal points intersect at the instants at which they are equal. Two temporal geometries or geographies, whose values are constant between their instants, intersect at the instants at which their values intersect, and two geographies intersect where their distance is zero. Geographies are supported as stated in .
The array form returns the pairs that intersect at some instant, with the periods during which they intersect.
Temporal touches
listitem.programlisting: tTouches({geometry,tgeom},{geometry,tgeom}) → tbool tTouchesPairs(tgeometry[],tgeometry[]) → setof(i integer,j integer,periods tstzspanset)
listitem.para: The array form returns the pairs of temporal geometries that touch at some instant, with the periods during which they touch.
